title: The Next Congress Needs to Reclaim Its Oversight of the Department of Defense
gist: Margaret Cassidy and Andrew Swick argue that while Congress has publicly deferred to the Trump administration's expansion of Pentagon power, the FY26 and FY27 NDAAs quietly embed funding fences, troop-floor certifications (76,000 in Europe, 28,500 in South Korea) and leadership-removal notification rules, which the administration has so far ignored without consequence. With Democrats likely to win the House and possibly the Senate in November, they expect a new Congress to use appropriations, confirmations, investigations and even impeachment to reassert control over defense strategy and budgets, noting the $1.5 trillion Pentagon request has already been trimmed.

insights.claim: The Trump administration has conducted strikes in Venezuela, expansive Caribbean maritime interdictions and a sustained offensive campaign against Iran with little congressional oversight or authorization.
insights.speaker: Margaret M. Cassidy and Andrew Swick
insights.so_what: Elevated geopolitical risk in oil-relevant regions with weak legislative constraints.

insights.claim: The administration has asserted heightened Department of Defense control over defense contractors and canceled or restructured major acquisition programs, possibly inconsistent with statutory and regulatory frameworks.
insights.speaker: Margaret M. Cassidy and Andrew Swick
insights.so_what: Defense primes and contractors face elevated program-cancellation and political-control risk.
insights.quote: defense contractors have been subjected to heightened Department of Defense control, which may be inconsistent with existing statutory and regulatory frameworks

insights.claim: The administration has removed senior civilian and uniformed leaders at an unprecedented pace, plans to merge Northern and Southern Command into a Western Hemisphere Command, and Hegseth has declared a 20 percent cut to the general/flag officer corps.
insights.speaker: Margaret M. Cassidy and Andrew Swick
insights.so_what: Pentagon institutional turbulence adds execution risk to programs and budgets.

insights.claim: Republican members of Congress acquiesce to executive power because they fear their voter bases and Trump-backed primary challenges, as shown by many high-profile primary losses by Republican incumbents this year.
insights.speaker: Margaret M. Cassidy and Andrew Swick
insights.so_what: Legislative checks on defense policy depend on electoral shifts rather than GOP defection.

insights.claim: The 2025 National Security Strategy narrowed U.S. global influence, prioritizing the Western Hemisphere, homeland defense, migration and economic security, framing China as a competitor to be managed and allies as transactional partners.
insights.speaker: Margaret M. Cassidy and Andrew Swick
insights.so_what: Allies face pressure to raise defense spending, supporting non-U.S. defense budgets.
insights.quote: allies were similarly viewed as transactional partners: pay more for defense or face less U.S. commitment

insights.claim: The 2026 National Defense Strategy under Elbridge Colby kept China as the pacing challenge with deterrence by denial and forward posture while folding in Western Hemisphere-first priorities, straddling competing imperatives.
insights.speaker: Margaret M. Cassidy and Andrew Swick
insights.so_what: Pacific-oriented capability programs retain strategic cover despite White House priorities.

insights.claim: Congress, through the FY26 NDAA and appropriations, has sustained a globally postured, competition-centric military with strong commitment to Europe, Ukraine and the Indo-Pacific, framing China, Russia, Iran and North Korea as an 'axis of aggressors.'
insights.speaker: Margaret M. Cassidy and Andrew Swick
insights.so_what: Congressional consensus supports sustained high defense toplines regardless of executive priorities.
insights.quote: the most dangerous threat environment since World War II

insights.claim: The FY26 NDAA mandates co-production, base integration and industrial collaboration with allies to maintain advantage over China, beyond prior bills' language.
insights.speaker: Margaret M. Cassidy and Andrew Swick
insights.so_what: Tailwind for allied co-production deals and multinational defense supply chains.

insights.claim: FY26 NDAA Section 1086 mandates a new defense technology-transfer framework and Foreign Military Sales reforms impose clearer timelines, expanded data sharing in AI, quantum and autonomy, and eligibility for non-program-of-record and commercial systems.
insights.speaker: Margaret M. Cassidy and Andrew Swick
insights.so_what: Could accelerate export revenue for U.S. defense-tech and commercial vendors selling to allies.
insights.locator: Further, despite the White House's distancing

insights.claim: The FY26 NDAA freezes funds for combatant command restructuring unless the Secretary of Defense certifies national-security benefit and allied consultation, and freezes Army funds for restructuring Joint Munitions Command and Sustainment Command pending a readiness report.
insights.speaker: Margaret M. Cassidy and Andrew Swick
insights.so_what: Funding fences slow reorganizations that could disrupt contracts.

insights.claim: The FY26 NDAA bars using FY26 funds to cut U.S. troop levels in Europe below 76,000 or in South Korea below 28,500 without certifications and allied consultation.
insights.speaker: Margaret M. Cassidy and Andrew Swick
insights.so_what: Legislated troop floors reduce tail risk of abrupt U.S. withdrawal from Europe and Korea.
insights.locator: The FY26 National Defense Authorization Act tightens

insights.claim: The FY26 NDAA requires notification and reasons within five days when the President removes a Joint Chiefs member or combatant commander, or the Secretary removes service Judge Advocate Generals, and the House FY27 draft extends this to any two-star-plus officer.
insights.speaker: Margaret M. Cassidy and Andrew Swick
insights.so_what: Creates a public record that can fuel future oversight and investigations.

insights.claim: The distinctive feature of the FY26 and FY27 NDAAs is the cumulative use of statutory mandates, funding fences and detailed reporting, showing a publicly deferential Congress quietly reclaiming institutional ground.
insights.speaker: Margaret M. Cassidy and Andrew Swick
insights.so_what: Congress retains latent leverage over defense posture that a new majority can activate.
insights.quote: a Congress that, while publicly deferential, is quietly reclaiming institutional ground

insights.claim: Hegseth fired senior leaders including Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George without the five-day notice or written explanation required by Section 911 of the FY26 NDAA, and removed officers from promotion lists in March, August and September 2026, with Congress responding only with lukewarm questions.
insights.speaker: Margaret M. Cassidy and Andrew Swick
insights.so_what: Statutory constraints on the Pentagon are currently unenforced, raising policy unpredictability.
insights.quote: The very provision Congress wrote to assert its oversight role was ignored without consequence.

insights.claim: The Pentagon announced it would move about 5,000 troops from Germany to Poland without explanation, and Hegseth suggested NATO-assigned troops may be redeployed to the Western Hemisphere, signaling a possible coming violation of the 76,000 Europe troop floor.
insights.speaker: Margaret M. Cassidy and Andrew Swick
insights.so_what: U.S. posture shifts in Europe could accelerate European rearmament spending.
insights.locator: On force posture, the department announced

insights.claim: OMB issued a Statement of Administration Policy opposing NDAA provisions limiting discretion over foreign policy, military leadership and force posture as unconstitutional interference with the commander in chief.
insights.speaker: Margaret M. Cassidy and Andrew Swick
insights.so_what: Sets up executive-legislative constitutional conflict over defense control.
insights.locator: Furthermore, the Office of Management and Budget

insights.claim: Congress cannot legally enforce statutory requirements over a disobedient executive and must instead use appropriations, oversight and impeachment; courts typically deny congressional standing or deem such disputes political questions.
insights.speaker: Margaret M. Cassidy and Andrew Swick
insights.so_what: Real constraint on the Pentagon will come through budgets, a direct channel to defense contractor revenue.
insights.quote: Congress cannot legally enforce its statutory requirements over a disobedient executive
insights.locator: While Congress has so far failed

insights.claim: The administration requested an unprecedented $1.5 trillion for the Pentagon, $1.15 trillion via regular appropriations and $350 billion via reconciliation, but the House approved $1.07 trillion in regular appropriations and only $73 billion in reconciliation, and the Senate delayed another reconciliation package until after the election.
insights.speaker: Margaret M. Cassidy and Andrew Swick
insights.so_what: Actual defense funding is running well below the request; the reconciliation tranche is at risk, relevant for contractor growth assumptions.
insights.quote: The administration’s unprecedented $1.5 trillion budget request for the Pentagon came in two stages
insights.locator: As Congress debates the FY27 budget

insights.claim: Sen. Mitch McConnell warned that relying on party-line reconciliation for defense funding threatens long-term reliability of defense funding.
insights.speaker: Margaret M. Cassidy and Andrew Swick
insights.so_what: Reconciliation-funded defense spending is less durable; discount it in multi-year forecasts.

insights.claim: The FY26 Consolidated Appropriations Act, passed in February after a four-day shutdown over DHS funding, was steered opaquely by Rep. Tom Cole with details withheld even from the administration, a quiet assertion of congressional funding power.
insights.speaker: Margaret M. Cassidy and Andrew Swick
insights.so_what: Appropriators retain independent control of defense line items.

insights.claim: The House passed its FY27 NDAA in July but Senate Democrats blocked the Senate version in protest over the Iran war and it has not advanced, and Congress adjourned until after the midterms.
insights.speaker: Margaret M. Cassidy and Andrew Swick
insights.so_what: Delayed NDAA raises odds of continuing resolutions and slower new-start programs.
insights.locator: Congress adjourned at the end of September

themes.theme: Iran war, midterms and the next Congress

insights.claim: Congress passed a Russia sanctions bill in September but Trump has already issued a waiver to it in Moscow's favor.
insights.speaker: Margaret M. Cassidy and Andrew Swick
insights.so_what: Sanctions on Russia are less binding than headlines suggest.
insights.locator: Congress adjourned at the end of September

insights.claim: The latest Senate effort to end the Iran war failed by two votes in September with four Senate and seven House Republicans supporting it, and vulnerable Republican candidates are calling to end the war to lower gas prices.
insights.speaker: Margaret M. Cassidy and Andrew Swick
insights.so_what: Political pressure to end the Iran war, partly over gasoline prices, is building.
insights.locator: The most recent effort to end the war

insights.claim: Democrats are likely to take the House in November and increasingly likely to take the Senate.
insights.speaker: Margaret M. Cassidy and Andrew Swick
insights.so_what: A Democratic Congress would raise oversight intensity over Pentagon spending and war policy.
insights.quote: Democrats are likely to take the House in the November elections, and increasingly likely to take the Senate as well

insights.claim: A new Congress should freeze funds, delay confirmations, use subpoenas, restrict funding for non-compliance and consider impeaching officials, including the president, while War Powers action is unlikely to succeed and would end up at the Supreme Court.
insights.speaker: Margaret M. Cassidy and Andrew Swick
insights.so_what: Expect 2027 oversight fights to target Pentagon funding lines, a source of budget uncertainty for contractors.
insights.quote: Congress can and should restrict funding if the administration does not comply with the statutes it has written.
